catalog_quote: The distinctions between long and short vowels and distinctions between tones (whether a syllable is spoken with a higher or lower voice pitch) are both important for correct pronunciation and for distinguishing the meanings of words in Ngamo. Native speakers of Ngamo, however, know the correct vowel lengths and tones of words without having to see them written, and like publications in Hausa, publications in Ngamo generally do not mark vowel length and tone. ... LOW TONES have a grave accent ( `) over the vowel, HIGH TONES have no accent marks, FALLING TONES have a circumflex accent ( ^), and RISING TONES, which are rare, have a hachek . ... A major source of difference between the Gudi and Yaya dialects is in the tones of words. new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngamo (both Gudi and Yaya dialects) is described as a two-level tone language (H, L; falling HL contour, rare rising LH) with contrastive vowel length; in Gudi every lexical tone pattern has shifted one tonal domain rightward (Great Ngamo Tone Shift) leaving default L initially and floating final tones. None of the first-hand descriptions (Schuh 2005, 2009; Schuh et al. 2009; Grubic 2015) says anything about word stress or accentual prominence, positive or negative.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal: proper names, ideophones, some recent Hausa/Bole loans resist the GNTS; Yaya has downstepped H.)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern lexical citation forms and phrase-level tone rules within the intonational phrase (Schuh 2009 §3-5); TBU is the mora (Schuh 2005:5). No word-stress domain is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern first-hand material (Schuh 2005/2009, Schuh et al. 2009, Grubic 2015) is primarily on the Gudi dialect of Ngamo (Gadaka area), with comparative data from the Yaya dialect; Schuh and Ibriszimow both note the two dialects differ enough in phonology (especially tone, because of the Gudi-only Great Ngamo Tone Shift) to border on separate languages. Glottolog ngam1282 covers both; no separate glottocodes for Gudi/Yaya are known to me.

sources.note: Introduction (pp. iii-v) states vowel length and tone (H unmarked, L grave, falling circumflex, rare rising) are lexically distinctive and marks them on every headword; Gudi vs Yaya differ mainly in tone. No mention of stress.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2005. Yobe State, Nigeria as a linguistic area (full version of paper in Proceedings of BLS 31). Ms., UCLA.
sources.note: Areal features (rightward tone spreading etc.); no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' as prominence.

sources.citation: Grubic, Mira. 2015. Focus and alternative sensitivity in Ngamo (West-Chadic). PhD dissertation, Universität Potsdam (urn:nbn:de:kobv:517-opus4-81666).
sources.note: §3.1 'Prosody' (p.47): 'Gudi Ngamo is a tone language with two tones, a high tone (H)... and a low tone (L)'; summarizes GNTS after Schuh; §4 reports a pilot f0/duration study (Genzel & Grubic 2011) finding focus prosodically unmarked. No statement about word stress; 'stress' appears only for German/English examples.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2009. Ngamo tones and clitics. Ms., UCLA, 46 pp. (retrieved via Wayback from www.linguistics.ucla.edu/people/schuh/Papers/)
sources.note: Nothing about stress/accent. Fullest description of Gudi (and briefly Yaya) Ngamo tone: two tones H/L, falling and rare rising contours, floating H diagnostics, downstep in Yaya, tone rules within the intonational phrase, clitic tones.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2005. Degemination, compensatory lengthening, and gemination in Gudi Ngamo. UCLA Working Papers in Linguistics 11 (revised ms.), 11 pp.
sources.note: No stress statement. Says 'Syllable weight is the basis of metricality in Ngamo and nearly all its West Chadic sisters and cousins' (re poetry/song and morphology, p.9 of WPL version), and that long vowels are excluded from closed syllables; nothing on word-level prominence.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2005. The Great Ngamo Tone Shift. Ms., UCLA (second revision, July 2005), 31 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Entirely about tone: Gudi Ngamo shifted every lexical tone one tonal domain to the right with default L on the initial domain; TBU = mora; H/L (+F, rare R) system; floating tones. The words 'stress'/'accent' occur only for diacritics (grave/acute accent). Notes syllable weight (light/heavy, one extra-heavy syllable) but no prominence statement.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2004. Ngamo verbal system (paradigm table). Ms., UCLA, 2 pp.
sources.note: Tone-marked verb paradigms only; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2003. Chadic overview. In M. L. Bender, G. Takács & D. Appleyard (eds.), Selected Comparative-Historical Afrasian Linguistic Studies in Memory of Igor M. Diakonoff, 55-60. München: LINCOM Europa.
sources.note: Family-level only: 'All Chadic languages are tone languages... By far the most common Chadic tone system has high (H) and low (L) level tones and a downdrift intonation pattern.' Nothing on stress, nothing Ngamo-specific.
